Vignette: Priya

Priya is a 42-year-old South Asian woman who works as a domestic housekeeper, moving between several homes in a quiet suburban neighborhood where she has built a steady, reliable reputation over the past decade. She is married, and by most outward measures her life has the appearance of stability — a husband who works long hours, two teenage children, a small apartment that she keeps immaculately clean. But for the past two years, since a man she knew only as a neighbor began following her, Priya has not felt safe anywhere.

It started gradually, the way these things often do. The man — a resident on one of the streets where she worked — began appearing wherever she was. At first she dismissed it as coincidence. He would be at the bus stop when she arrived in the mornings. Then outside the grocery store. Then parked slowly past the home where she was cleaning, watching through the window. He left notes tucked under the windshield wiper of her employer's car, notes with her name on them. He called her phone from numbers she didn't recognize, breathing quietly before hanging up. For months, Priya told herself she was imagining it, that she was being foolish, that a woman like her — a maid, she says with a kind of tired resignation — should not make trouble. She said nothing to her employers. She said nothing to her husband until the man appeared outside her apartment building one evening and her daughter saw him standing there.

When she finally went to the police, the experience left her feeling more exposed than protected. The man was spoken to, warned, and the calls stopped. But Priya did not stop waiting for them to start again.

Now, two years later, she moves through her days in a state of constant readiness that exhausts her. She travels to her cleaning jobs by a route she changes every week. She no longer takes the same bus at the same time. When she is inside a client's home, she checks the windows repeatedly — not because she is cleaning them, but because she needs to see who is outside. Her employers have noticed that she sometimes stops mid-task and stands very still, listening. She cannot explain this to them, so she laughs it off and keeps working.

At night, sleep rarely comes easily. When it does, she wakes from dreams in which she is being watched through glass, unable to move or call out. She lies in the dark afterward, certain she has heard something in the hallway, and does not go back to sleep. Her husband tries to reassure her and she nods, but she does not believe him. She has come to understand, in a way she cannot fully articulate, that reassurance is not the same as safety.

She has pulled away from the small community of women she used to meet with on weekends — other South Asian women, friends she has known for years. She tells herself she is too tired, but the truth is that she does not want to be in public spaces where she cannot control who might walk in. She does not want to explain herself. There is also a shame she carries quietly, a feeling that she should have done something sooner, that she invited this somehow, though she cannot say how.

What strikes her most, she says, is how ordinary everything looks from the outside. She still shows up to work. She still makes dinner. She still folds laundry and helps with homework and smiles at her employers when they thank her. But inside, she is always somewhere else — standing at that window, reading that note, watching a car slow down on a street she thought was safe.

She describes herself as a woman who used to feel invisible in a way that was comfortable. Now she feels watched even when no one is there.
